summary: EU home affairs commissioner Ylva Johansson confirmed the Commission is investigating whether its microtargeted X ad campaign promoting the CSAM-scanning proposal broke the Digital Services Act, but she deflected MEPs' detailed questions at a LIBE committee hearing. The article also covers allegations of commercial lobbying, her list of meetings with tech firms and child safety groups, and her defence that the proposal is technology neutral and not mass surveillance.
one_line: Ylva Johansson confirmed a DSA probe into the Commission's microtargeted CSAM-law ads on X but avoided answering MEPs' questions at a LIBE hearing.
key_facts: Ylva Johansson, EU home affairs commissioner, confirmed the Commission is investigating whether its microtargeted ad campaign for the CSAM-scanning proposal broke the Digital Services Act (DSA).
The DSA prohibits targeting ads using sensitive personal data such as political opinions; X was designated a Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) by the Commission in April.
Technologist Danny Mekić spotted the campaign, and his findings ran in the Dutch newspaper De Volkskrant.

The ads targeted users in the Netherlands, Sweden, Belgium, Finland, Slovenia, Portugal and the Czech Republic, countries not supportive of the proposal per leaked minutes of a September 14 European Council meeting.
Mekić said X's Transparency Report showed ads were excluded from people interested in Julian Assange, 'nexit', 'brexit', 'spanexit', Victor Orbán, Nigel Farage, AfD, and also Christianity.

On October 13, 2023 Johansson tweeted that her department followed the guidelines and the law '100%', but later told the LIBE committee she had received 'new information' about possible DSA compliance questions.
Johansson declined to give details of the campaign, saying it was for her 'service' to answer, but agreed to respond in writing 'as soon as possible'.
MEP Sophie in 't Veld said 'the end doesn't justify the means' and that privileged channels exist for the Commission to communicate with legislators, not an ad campaign on Twitter.

Journalist Apostolis Fotiadis, co-author of a BalkanInsight investigation, said emails between DG-Home officials and a 'key stakeholder' showed 'privileged access' and cooperation going 'way beyond' consultation.

Johansson said she met Google six times; Microsoft, Meta and TikTok three times each; Twitter (X) twice; Apple and Amazon once each; Thorn and Brave Movement twice each; Tech Alliance and ICANN once each.
Johansson said the proposal is 'technology neutral' and denied that only Thorn and Microsoft have the necessary scanning technology.
She said detection is allowed only after prevention fails and a court decision, and cited 5.2 million videos, pictures and grooming attempts reported, 70% from private communication.

The European Data Protection Supervisor's seminar earlier in the week, which Johansson declined to attend, heard 20+ speakers raise deep misgivings, with the EDPS warning of a tipping point for freedom and democracy.
